2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Transmittal Letter Transmittal June 25, 2026 Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council, We are pleased to present the 2026–2028 Biennial Budget and 2026–2031 Capital Improvement Program (CIP). Together, these planning documents provide the financial framework necessary to support the City’s full range of municipal services and long-term infrastructure investments. The Biennial Budget and CIP support essential community services including public safety; maintenance and improvement of streets, parks, storm drainage systems, and other public infrastructure; recreational programs and human services; environmental stewardship; planning, zoning, economic and community development activities; emergency preparedness; code enforcement; and core administrative functions such as finance, human resources, and information technology. Property Tax, Sales Tax, Transaction and Use Tax (Measure GG), and Utility Users Tax continue to serve as stable core revenues, with modest growth projected in the upcoming years compared to prior budget cycles. The Transient Occupancy Tax (TOT) rate was recently increased from 10% to 14%, effective January 2025 with the passage of Measure LL, and will help support infrastructure. Other revenues, including permits, licenses, service charges, and recreation program fees, continue to trend favorably following fee updates implemented through the City’s 2024 Comprehensive User Fee and Cost Allocation Study, along with annual Consumer Price Index (CPI) adjustments. A comprehensive Recreation and Community Services cost-of-service and market analysis is currently underway. Accordingly, the biennial budget does not include a full update to Recreation and Community Services fees at this time. Future revenue projections may be refined following completion of the fee study and subsequent City Council consideration of the recommended adjustments. Investment earnings are also contributing to steady revenue growth, despite interest rates coming down from the Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 high average yield of 5.18% to now 4.05%. As of April 2026, the California Asset Management Program (CAMP) rate was 3.77% and Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) was 3.83% (each down from 4.23% and 4.17% earlier in the fiscal year, respectively). The operating budgets for FY 2027 and FY 2028 reflect cautious optimism as geopolitical and economic factors impact both revenue growth and expenditure growth. While the City’s fiscal condition remains stable, the cost of providing municipal services continues to increase, particularly in utilities, contractual services, consultant support, insurance, and other operational expenditures. Maintaining local fiscal flexibility and preserving the City’s ability to respond to community priorities remain key budget objectives, ensuring Newark can continue delivering high-quality services while maintaining prudent and sustainable financial practices. This budget includes funding the following City priorities as elaborated in the Strategic Priority Areas section: Foster a Safe and Healthy Community Further Economic Vitality and Housing for All Boost Financial Resilience and Excellence in Service Delivery Modernize Public Facilities and Infrastructure Strengthen Community through Education and Engagement 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Transmittal Letter Specifically, the City has focused on long-term strategic planning initiatives, including the development or update of strategic plans related to City facilities, parks, public art, transportation, broadband infrastructure, climate action and sustainability, hazard mitigation, emergency preparedness, and services and response strategies for the unhoused community. These planning efforts evaluate existing assets and service levels, incorporate community outreach and stakeholder engagement, and apply industry best practices to identify immediate, mid-term, and long-term strategies to address evolving community needs and infrastructure priorities. Consistent with the 2025 Community Survey results, residents continue to identify infrastructure maintenance, traffic circulation, parks and recreational amenities, development services, and emergency preparedness as top City service priorities. These priorities continue to guide the City’s operational planning, capital investment strategies, and longterm financial planning efforts. The first year of the Capital Improvement Program includes 61 new projects totaling approximately $32.4 million across infrastructure, parks, facilities, equipment, technology, and planning initiatives. Major infrastructure investments include approximately $9.3 million for projects such as the Thornton Avenue Pavement Overlays, Old Town Priority Development Area (PDA) Streetscape Improvements, and Broadband Initiative. Planned park improvement projects total approximately $8.0 million and include the Birch Grove Park Playground, Newark Community Park All Abilities Playground, and new park signage improvements. Facilities-related projects total approximately $4.9 million and include various facility improvements, as well as initial planning and construction activities associated with the Fire Stations 27 and 29 Reconstruction Project. The CIP also includes approximately $1.3 million in equipment replacement and acquisition, primarily supporting Police and Public Works operations. In addition, approximately $1.9 million is allocated toward planning and policy studies, including the Urban Forest Master Plan, Four Corners Area Plan, and NewPark Place Specific Plan Enhancement, funded through the Community Development Maintenance Fee Fund. In FY 2028, the second fiscal year of the Capital Improvement Program, 16 projects are planned totaling approximately $7.9 million. Key projects include Pedestrian Hybrid Beacon installations, Traffic Signal Interconnect improvements, sports field lighting and amenity upgrades, initial work associated with the Service Center Administrative Building Replacement Project, and various Public Works and Police equipment replacement projects. FY 2027 Budget Highlights The FY 2027 General Fund Operating Budget totals approximately $92.2 million, compared to the FY 2026 projected expenditure level of $97.5 million and the FY 2026 Amended Budget of $97.6 million. The reduction is primarily attributable to one-time General Fund transfers made in FY 2026 to support capital projects and infrastructure investments within the Capital Improvement Program. Future transfers to support capital projects will continue to be evaluated annually based on year-end operating results, reserve levels, infrastructure priorities, and overall fiscal conditions. Personnel expenditures are projected at approximately $47.6 million and continue to represent the City’s largest operating expenditure category. Personnel costs reflect negotiated labor agreements, pension obligations, healthcare costs, inflationary adjustments, and strategic staffing investments necessary to maintain service levels and respond to increasing operational demands. Non-personnel expenditures are budgeted at approximately $24.3 million and include contractual services, materials and supplies, utilities, travel and training, technology costs, and internal service fund allocations. While inflationary pressures continue to impact operational costs, departments have continued to exercise prudent spending controls and cost management efforts where feasible. The Alameda County Fire Department (ACFD) service contract is projected at approximately $15.4 million in FY 2027, reflecting continued regional public safety cost escalation. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Transmittal Letter In FY 2027, the City will also initiate a community-focused branding effort intended to help develop and strengthen Newark’s civic identity and community engagement efforts. In addition, the budget includes targeted staffing additions, including a Senior Management Analyst, two Administrative Support Specialists, a Principal Planner, and two Recreation Assistants. These positions are intended to support increasing service demands, operational workloads, development activity, and organizational capacity across multiple departments. The budget also includes funding to initiate a Public Works organizational and service level assessment. The assessment will evaluate operational needs, staffing alignment, service delivery expectations, and long-term infrastructure maintenance requirements as the City’s Capital Improvement Program and operational demands continue to expand. The assessment is intended to help identify opportunities to improve operational efficiency, organizational alignment, and long-term service sustainability. FY 2028 Budget Highlights The FY 2028 General Fund Operating Budget totals approximately $96.7 million, reflecting an increase of approximately $4.5 million over the FY 2027 Budget. The increase is primarily attributable to projected inflationary cost escalation, including personnel costs, public safety services, utilities, contractual services, and other ongoing operational expenditures. Staffing levels are projected to remain generally consistent with FY 2027 and may be adjusted in future years based on operational needs, service demands, economic conditions, and City Council priorities. To support the City’s expanding Capital Improvement Program (CIP) and long-term infrastructure initiatives, the budget includes a limited-term CIP Manager position to strengthen project management capacity and support implementation of the City’s transition from a two-year CIP to a five-year CIP planning framework. The position will assist in coordinating major capital initiatives, including the Fire Stations 27 and 29 Reconstruction Project, and ongoing planning efforts associated with a future Cultural Arts Center. The budget also includes funding for a Public Works organizational and service level assessment to evaluate operational needs, staffing alignment, service delivery expectations, and long-term infrastructure maintenance requirements. Together, these efforts are intended to strengthen operational efficiency, organizational alignment, project delivery capacity, and long-term service sustainability as the City’s infrastructure responsibilities, facility needs, and capital program continue to expand. In Closing While economic uncertainty, geopolitical instability, and inflationary pressures continue to present challenges, the 2026–2028 Biennial Budget and Five-Year Capital Improvement Program position the City to continue delivering core services, advancing critical infrastructure investments, and maintaining prudent financial stewardship. The budget reflects the City’s commitment to balancing City Council priorities, emerging community needs, operational sustainability, and long-term fiscal resilience while continuing to provide high-quality services to the Newark community through conservative and strategic financial planning. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Transmittal Letter Acknowledgments The preparation of the 2026–2028 Biennial Budget and 2026-2031 Capital Improvement Program reflects a collaborative effort across all City departments. It is located 35 miles south of San Francisco, 25 miles south of Oakland, and 20 miles north of San Jose. With a growing population of over 46,903 residents, the City of Newark offers a small town feel while sitting in the heart of bustling Silicon Valley. The City occupies an area of approximately fourteen square miles. Past The City’s roots are over 150 years old. By California’s statehood in 1850, landings along the Bay in the vicinity of today’s City of Newark had already began to appear. In 1853, Mayhew’s Landing included warehouses for wheat, hay, and coal. This activity triggered interest in the surrounding area and by 1856 the Mayhew Ranch included 1,500 acres of farmland extending inland to present-day I-880. In the 1870s, a swamp reclamation project was started and an English capitalist bought an interest in the property. The land was eventually bought out by a Scotsman who named the City ‘Newark’, after the castle ‘Newark’ in Port Glasgow, Scotland. Work started on a railroad through the townsite in 1875. The South Pacific Coast Railroad was not only completed from Dumbarton Point south all the way to Santa Cruz, but the town site was also moved to coincide with the curve on the railroad where the tracks turned south toward San Jose. Eventually, the railroad was extended north from Newark to Alameda, providing direct ferry service to San Francisco. The completion of the railroad precipitated additional development in Newark. Hotels and stores were soon erected, along with some of the first manufacturing industries. These enterprises joined the production of salt, which had been underway in the Newark area since the 1850’s. Acquisitions and mergers of salt production companies throughout the Bay Area ultimately resulted in the formation of today’s Cargill Salt. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA History of the City Through the years, residents in Newark have retained a strong sense of independence and community. In 1953, a group representing the chambers of commerce of Centerville, Irvington, Mission San Jose, Niles, Warm Springs, and Newark commissioned a study to incorporate all six communities into one City. However, the Newark Chamber of Commerce began its own movement toward incorporation of just Newark. In September 1955, this effort paid off with the incorporation of Newark as the first new city in Alameda County in 47 years and defeating the effort to incorporate Newark as part of the Fremont metropolis. Present Newark has evolved throughout the years from its days enriched in agriculture, manufacturing, and railroad to today’s expansion of high-tech, bio-tech, advanced manufacturing, and the health sciences. Newark represents a diverse, bustling economy at the gateway to some of the world’s affluent markets. Small town values remain, and lower housing and development costs, close proximity to skilled workforce and universities, and a regionally strategic location make Newark a prime site for growth. The City is a general law city and operates under the Council-Manager form of government. Under this form of government, policy-making and legislative authority are vested in a five-member elected City Council consisting of the Mayor and four Council Members. The Mayor and City Council have responsibility for passing ordinances, adopting and amending the operating and capital budgets, appointing various committee members, and hiring both the City Manager and City Attorney. The City Manager is responsible for carrying out the policies and ordinances established by the City Council, for overseeing the day-to-day operations of the City, and for appointing the various department heads. The City provides a full range of municipal services to its community. These include public safety; construction and maintenance of streets, parks, storm drains, and other infrastructure; recreational activities and human services; planning, zoning, and other community, and economic development activities; emergency preparedness; code enforcement; and administrative services such as human resources, information technology, and finance. Each fund is a separate self-balancing accounting entity established to account for specific activities or objectives in accordance with legal, regulatory, grant, contractual, or operational requirements. The City annually evaluates its fund structure to determine whether funds with similar purposes may be consolidated for financial reporting purposes to improve transparency, efficiency, accountability, and clarity. The funds presented in this budget are maintained and reported as separate funds. In accordance with governmental accounting standards, City funds are classified into three categories: Governmental Funds, Proprietary Funds, and Fiduciary Funds. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Fund Structure Governmental Funds Governmental Funds account for basic governmental services traditionally associated with municipal operations, including public safety, public works, recreation, community development, and general government functions. These funds are primarily supported through taxes, intergovernmental revenues, permits, service charges, and other nonexchange revenues. Governmental Funds are further categorized as General Fund, Special Revenue Funds, Capital Project Funds, and Debt Service Funds. General Fund (110) The General Fund is the City’s primary operating fund and accounts for activities not required to be reported in another fund. Major revenue sources include property taxes, sales and use taxes, utility users taxes, business license taxes, franchise fees, permits, and other general governmental revenues. General Fund expenditures support core municipal services, including City Council, City Administration, Police, Fire, Community Development, Recreation and Community Services, Public Works, and other general governmental operations. Other General Fund Operating Funds Paramedic Tax Fund (111) Accounts for revenues and expenditures associated with the voter-approved Paramedic Tax Program supporting Fire Department paramedic services, training, equipment, supplies, and related operational costs. Transaction and Use Tax Fund (112) Accounts for revenues and expenditures associated with Measure GG, the City’s voter-approved one-half cent transactions and use tax measure approved in 2016. Utility Users Tax Fund (115) Accounts for revenues and expenditures associated with the City’s Utility Users Tax (UUT) Ordinance. The UUT is a voter-approved general tax imposed at a rate of 3.25% on electricity, natural gas, telecommunications, video, and related utility services consumed within the City. Measure PP, approved by Newark voters in 2020, extended the UUT through December 31, 2029. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Fund Structure General Fund Cost Centers General Fund Cost Centers account for activities where fees or charges are intended to partially or fully recover the cost of providing services. In practice, certain services are not fully cost recoverable due to market conditions, affordability considerations, or community benefit objectives established by the City Council. General Fund contributions may therefore supplement user fee revenues to maintain service levels and community access. Development Cost Center (120) Accounts for Community Development, Planning, Engineering, and Building activities associated with private development and construction within the City. Operations are supported primarily through permits, plan check fees, inspection fees, and other development-related charges. Recreation Cost Center (130) Accounts for recreation programs, aquatic services, childcare, senior services, wellness programs, and other community-based recreational activities. Operations are funded primarily through user fees and program revenues, supplemented by General Fund support to maintain community access, affordability, and desired service levels. Maintenance Cost Center (140) Accounts for the maintenance, repair, and preservation of City infrastructure and public facilities, including streets, park and landscape maintenance, street lighting, weed abatement, and environmental services. Operations are supported through General Fund contributions and other available funding sources to maintain the safety, functionality, and long-term condition of public assets. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Fund Structure General Fund Reserves The City maintains General Fund reserves to support long-term fiscal sustainability, operational continuity, cash flow stability, and financial resiliency. Reserve levels are guided by the City’s Fund Balance and Reserve Policy and informed by Government Finance Officers Association best practices. Reserves provide financial flexibility to address economic uncertainty, emergencies, deferred maintenance, long-term liabilities, and strategic capital needs while maintaining stable municipal services. Emergency and Economic Uncertainty Reserve (101/102) The Emergency and Economic Uncertainty Reserve is the City’s primary unrestricted fiscal stabilization reserve. This reserve provides funding capacity for unforeseen emergencies, natural disasters, legal liabilities, revenue shortfalls, economic downturns, or other unexpected fiscal disruptions impacting City operations. The reserve supports continuity of essential public services, mitigates operational risk, and provides financial flexibility during periods of economic volatility or one-time fiscal stress. Pension and Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB) Reserve (103) Provides funding for pension obligations, Section 115 Trust contributions, retiree health obligations, and other longterm workforce-related liabilities. The reserve supports long-term cost management, reduces exposure to market volatility, and improves budget stability and financial sustainability. Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) The Five-Year Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) serves as the City’s long-term plan for maintaining and enhancing public infrastructure, facilities, and community assets. The CIP provides the framework for prioritizing capital investments, aligning funding with City Council strategic priorities, and ensuring fiscal accountability across multiple fiscal years. These policies are aligned with Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) best practices and are intended to guide the preparation, adoption, and administration of the City’s Biennial Budget. Budget and Financial Planning Policies The City’s Biennial Budget is developed to support long-term fiscal sustainability, operational stability, service delivery objectives, infrastructure needs, and City Council priorities. The City shall adopt and maintain a structurally balanced budget in which recurring revenues and available financing sources are sufficient to fund recurring operating expenditures. Budget development shall incorporate long-range financial planning, operational needs, infrastructure obligations, economic conditions, and City Council priorities to support ongoing fiscal sustainability. Revenue projections shall be developed using conservative, yet realistic assumptions based on historical trends, economic indicators, development activity, inflationary factors, and other relevant financial data. The City utilizes a hybrid budgeting methodology incorporating line-item, incremental, and position-based budgeting principles, supplemented by performance considerations and long-range financial planning to support operational accountability, strategic planning, and long-term fiscal sustainability. Incremental budgeting shall generally be utilized for ongoing operating expenditures, with the prior year budget serving as the baseline and adjusted for known operational, contractual, inflationary, and service-level changes. Position-based budgeting shall be utilized for personnel expenditures, with salary and benefit costs developed based on authorized staffing positions, labor agreements, retirement obligations, projected vacancies, and other personnel-related cost factors. Performance, operational, and service-level considerations may be incorporated into the budget development process to support organizational accountability, resource allocation, and City Council priorities. The Biennial Budget shall be coordinated with the Five-Year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) and Five-Year Financial Forecast to evaluate the long-term sustainability of revenues, expenditures, reserves, capital infrastructure, pension and OPEB obligations, debt commitments, and other long-range financial needs. General Fund and other major fund balances shall be maintained at levels sufficient to support cash flow requirements, operational stability, financial contingencies, and economic uncertainties. Departments are responsible for operating within adopted appropriations, approved staffing levels, and applicable budgetary authority. Budget adjustments requiring additional appropriations shall require City Council approval in accordance with the Municipal Code and adopted financial policies. Unexpended appropriations shall lapse at fiscal year-end unless associated with legally encumbered obligations, approved contracts, active capital projects, or other authorized commitments supported by prior approved appropriations. Eligible appropriations may be administratively carried forward into subsequent fiscal years, subject to funding availability and compliance with applicable budgetary and purchasing authority requirements. One-time or nonrecurring revenues should generally not be used to fund ongoing operating expenditures and should instead be prioritized for capital improvements, reserves, pension or OPEB obligations, debt reduction, or other nonrecurring purposes. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Financial Policies Financial Forecasting and Long-Range Planning Policies The City shall utilize multi-year financial forecasting and long-range planning practices to evaluate fiscal sustainability, identify emerging financial risks, and support informed policy and budget decisions. Long-range financial planning shall consider economic conditions, revenue trends, infrastructure and capital needs, labor and pension obligations, service demands, inflationary pressures, debt commitments, reserve levels, and other operational or strategic factors affecting the City’s long-term fiscal condition. The Five-Year Financial Forecast shall serve as a planning tool to evaluate future revenues, expenditures, reserve levels, capital funding needs, and long-term liabilities, identify structural budget trends, and support informed decision-making by the City Council and City management. The City shall periodically update long-range financial projections to reflect changes in economic conditions, legislation, labor agreements, development activity, infrastructure requirements, and other significant financial or operational assumptions impacting the City’s fiscal outlook. Revenue Management and Cost Recovery Policies The City shall utilize conservative yet realistic revenue forecasting practices and monitor major revenue sources throughout the fiscal year to support fiscal stability and informed financial planning. Revenue forecasts shall incorporate historical trends, economic conditions, development activity, assessed valuation growth, sales tax performance, consumer activity, inflationary factors, and other relevant financial data. User fees, service charges, and development-related fees shall be periodically reviewed and updated in accordance with the City’s adopted Cost Recovery Policy, City Council direction, and applicable legal requirements. The City may periodically conduct comprehensive user fee, development impact fee, and cost allocation studies to evaluate service costs, cost recovery levels, market conditions, and administrative cost allocations. Fees and service charges shall generally not exceed the reasonable cost of providing services, including applicable direct and indirect costs, unless otherwise authorized by law. The City shall strive to align fees and charges for fee-supported operations and enterprise-like activities with the full cost of service delivery, including operations, maintenance, capital replacement, administrative support, and debt obligations, where appropriate. Fee structures may consider factors including cost recovery objectives, market comparability, community benefit, accessibility, equity considerations, legal limitations, and administrative feasibility. Fees and service charges may be adjusted periodically based on changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), labor costs, operating costs, market conditions, or updated cost-of-service analyses. Where fees have not been adjusted for extended periods or where significant increases are necessary to achieve cost recovery objectives, phased implementation strategies may be considered to reduce sudden financial impacts on residents, businesses, and service users. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Financial Policies Expenditure Management Policies The City shall manage expenditures in a manner that supports long-term fiscal sustainability, operational stability, and alignment between ongoing service levels and available recurring revenues. Expenditure growth, including labor, pension, insurance, utilities, contractual services, maintenance, and other operating costs, shall be monitored and evaluated as part of the City’s multi-year financial planning process. Departments are responsible for managing expenditures within adopted appropriations, authorized staffing levels, and applicable budgetary authority, while identifying operational efficiencies and cost-effective service delivery practices where feasible. Ongoing expenditure commitments and service level impacts shall be evaluated in the context of the City’s longrange financial outlook, projected revenue growth, operational needs, and overall fiscal sustainability. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Financial Policies Reserve and Fund Balance Policies The City shall maintain reserves and fund balances in accordance with the City’s adopted Fund Balance and Reserve Policy to support fiscal stability, operational continuity, cash flow requirements, emergency response, economic uncertainty, long-term liabilities, capital infrastructure needs, and overall financial resilience. Reserve levels shall be periodically evaluated using a GFOA-informed fiscal risk assessment methodology that considers revenue volatility, expenditure trends, liquidity needs, unfunded liabilities, infrastructure conditions, economic conditions, and long-range financial planning considerations. The City strives to maintain Emergency and Fiscal Uncertainty Reserves in accordance with reserve targets established under the City’s adopted Fund Balance and Reserve Policy. Reserve usage shall be limited to maintaining service continuity, addressing unforeseen financial obligations, responding to emergencies or economic downturns, mitigating revenue shortfalls, and supporting other strategic financial needs approved by the City Council. When reserve levels fall below established targets, the City shall strive to restore reserves over a reasonable multi-year period consistent with the City’s long-range financial plan. Additional reserves and assigned or committed fund balances may be maintained for pension and OPEB obligations, infrastructure and facilities maintenance, equipment and technology replacement, capital improvements, self-insurance, debt management, economic stabilization, and other strategic or long-term financial purposes as determined by the City Council. The City may maintain a Section 115 Pension Rate Stabilization and OPEB Trust (“Section 115 Trust”) to prefund pension and retiree healthcare obligations, mitigate contribution volatility, improve long-term budget predictability, strengthen financial flexibility, and reduce unfunded liabilities associated with CalPERS and OPEB obligations. The Section 115 Trust shall be administered in accordance with applicable Internal Revenue Service regulations, California Government Code Sections 53216 and 53620, GASB requirements, trust agreements, investment policies, and applicable City Council actions. The Section 115 Trust is intended to function as a long-term pension and OPEB stabilization tool and shall not replace prudent General Fund reserves or be used to address unrelated structural operating deficits. Consistent with applicable legal and fiduciary requirements, trust assets may be strategically utilized to stabilize pension contribution volatility, reimburse eligible pension or OPEB expenditures, improve General Fund liquidity, support long-range financial planning, and preserve funding capacity for strategic capital and infrastructure investments. The City may periodically evaluate discretionary contributions, accelerated unfunded liability payments, pension stabilization strategies, reimbursement approaches, funding corridors, and other prefunding methodologies intended to improve funded status, reduce long-term costs, and support fiscal sustainability objectives. Funding decisions may consider year-end operating surpluses, salary savings, one-time revenues, favorable pension contribution variances, reserve levels, capital needs, economic conditions, and long-range financial forecast assumptions. The Maintenance Reserve Fund may be maintained to support the maintenance, repair, rehabilitation, replacement, and preservation of City facilities, buildings, parks, streets, utilities, technology systems, and other infrastructure assets necessary to maintain operational reliability, public safety, and long-term asset sustainability. Equipment and technology replacement reserves may be maintained to support the planned replacement and lifecycle management of vehicles, heavy equipment, public safety equipment, technology infrastructure, cybersecurity systems, and other operational assets necessary to maintain reliable and efficient service delivery. Transfers to, from, or between reserves, assigned fund balances, and Section 115 Trust accounts shall be evaluated in conjunction with the City’s annual and biennial budget process, long-range financial planning efforts, capital planning activities, reserve targets, and fiscal sustainability objectives, and shall be subject to applicable City Council approvals, policies, and legal requirements. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Financial Policies Capital Improvement Program Policies The City shall maintain a multi-year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) to support infrastructure preservation, regulatory compliance, public safety, operational needs, and strategic community investments. The CIP shall incorporate long-term infrastructure planning, asset management principles, fiscal sustainability, and City Council priorities to support sustainable infrastructure investment and service delivery. Capital projects shall be evaluated and prioritized using objective and transparent criteria consistent with Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) best practices and the City’s adopted CIP prioritization methodology. Evaluation criteria may include public safety, legal and regulatory requirements, asset condition, operational necessity, service impacts, infrastructure preservation, operational efficiencies, project readiness, funding availability, environmental sustainability, community benefit, and alignment with strategic goals and City Council priorities. The City may utilize project ranking systems, prioritization scorecards, asset condition assessments, and other capital planning tools to support transparent, data-informed, and strategically aligned capital investment decisions. Capital investment planning shall consider lifecycle costs, ongoing maintenance obligations, operating impacts, staffing implications, replacement needs, and long-term fiscal sustainability. Capital improvements may be funded through available fund balances, impact fees, grants, debt financing, dedicated revenues, development-related funding sources, and other legally available funding mechanisms. Capital projects and capital asset expenditures shall be evaluated in accordance with the City’s adopted capitalization policy, applicable accounting standards, and administrative procedures. Capitalization thresholds may be periodically reviewed to support operational efficiency, asset management objectives, financial reporting accuracy, and effective administration of the Capital Improvement Program. Debt Management Policies The City may utilize debt financing as a strategic financing tool for capital improvements, infrastructure, equipment, and other long-term assets that provide ongoing public benefit and support City Council priorities. Debt shall be issued prudently and only when determined to be financially feasible, legally permissible, and consistent with the City’s adopted Capital Improvement Program, operating budget, and long-range financial plans. Prior to issuing debt, the City shall evaluate affordability, repayment capacity, revenue stability, reserve levels, operating and maintenance impacts, existing and projected debt obligations, and long-term fiscal sustainability. Debt financing shall generally be limited to projects or assets with useful lives that approximate or exceed the related repayment period. The City shall not issue long-term debt to finance ongoing operating expenditures, recurring personnel costs, routine maintenance, or structural operating deficits. The City shall evaluate alternative funding sources, including grants, impact fees, development contributions, reserves, pay-as-you-go financing, and available cash funding, prior to issuing debt. Refunding or refinancing opportunities may be considered when they produce economic benefit, improve debt service structure, enhance operational flexibility, or support other strategic financial objectives. The City shall seek to preserve strong financial management practices, maintain financial flexibility and creditworthiness, minimize borrowing costs, and comply with all applicable federal and state laws, disclosure requirements, and adopted debt management procedures. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Financial Policies Pension and OPEB Funding Policies The City shall proactively manage pension and Other Post-Employment Benefit (OPEB) obligations through long-range financial planning, actuarially informed funding strategies, and ongoing evaluation of long-term liabilities and funding requirements. Pension and OPEB funding strategies shall consider actuarially determined contributions, unfunded liability trends, investment performance, demographic assumptions, operating impacts, and long-term fiscal sustainability. The City may utilize pension stabilization reserves, OPEB trust funds, Section 115 Trust assets, and other prefunding strategies to support long-term liability management, contribution stability, and fiscal sustainability. The City may periodically evaluate discretionary contributions, accelerated unfunded liability payments, prefunding strategies, and other funding approaches intended to improve funded status and reduce long-term costs. Pension and OPEB obligations, reserve funding levels, actuarial assumptions, and long-term liability trends shall be periodically reviewed as part of the City’s multi-year financial planning and reserve evaluation process. Pension and OPEB trust assets shall be managed in accordance with applicable trust agreements, investment policies, fiduciary standards, and prudent long-term investment practices intended to balance risk, liquidity, and long-term return objectives. Investment and Cash Management Policies City funds shall be invested in accordance with the City’s annually adopted Investment Policy, applicable provisions of the California Government Code, and prudent public fund management practices. The primary objectives of the City’s investment program, in order of priority, shall be preservation of principal, maintenance of adequate liquidity, and prudent investment yield. The City shall maintain sufficient liquidity to meet operational cash flow requirements, payroll obligations, debt service payments, capital expenditures, and other financial commitments. Investments shall be managed in a manner that emphasizes safety, liquidity, diversification, and prudent risk management while seeking market-appropriate returns within legal and policy limitations. Investment maturities and portfolio structure shall be managed to align with anticipated cash flow requirements and minimize exposure to market, credit, and interest rate risk. The City shall diversify investments by security type, maturity, issuer, financial institution, and investment strategy to reduce portfolio risk and maintain prudent investment practices. The City shall utilize the prudent investor standard in managing public funds and investment activities, recognizing the importance of managing investments within the context of the overall portfolio and long-term financial objectives. Investment activities shall incorporate appropriate internal controls, segregation of responsibilities, safekeeping procedures, and oversight practices to protect public funds and ensure compliance with applicable laws, fiduciary standards, and adopted policies. Authorized investments, financial institutions, and investment counterparties shall be limited to those permitted under the City’s Investment Policy and applicable provisions of California law. Investment performance and portfolio compliance shall be periodically monitored and reported in accordance with the City’s Investment Policy and applicable legal reporting requirements. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Financial Policies Authorized Position List Administration Policies The City maintains personnel administration policies intended to support operational efficiency, workforce flexibility, fiscal sustainability, and effective public service delivery consistent with the City’s Personnel Rules and Regulations. The City shall maintain centralized position control through the adopted budget process. No increases to authorized citywide staffing levels, or material ongoing staffing expansions shall occur without City Council approval through the budget process or separate City Council action. Consistent with the City’s adopted Classification Plan, Compensation Plan or Salary Schedule, Personnel Rules and Regulations, applicable labor agreements, and adopted budget appropriations, the City Manager and Personnel Officer may administer routine personnel actions involving existing authorized and budgeted positions necessary to support operational and service delivery needs. Routine personnel actions may include position allocations, reclassifications, transfers, advancement within approved flexibly staffed classification series, retitles, revisions to classification specifications, and other staffing adjustments within existing total authorized citywide staffing levels and adopted appropriations. Such actions shall be reviewed in consultation with the Finance Director and Human Resources Director, as appropriate. Consistent with the Personnel Rules and Regulations, the City Manager or designee may create, revise, consolidate, or abolish classifications as necessary to support organizational and operational needs, provided such actions do not increase total authorized citywide staffing levels or materially increase ongoing fiscal obligations without City Council approval. Personnel actions involving material organizational restructuring, creation of additional supervisory, management, or executive layers, significant compensation impacts, amendments to compensation plans or salary schedules, changes to benefit structures, authorized staffing positions, or actions materially affecting longterm fiscal obligations shall require City Council approval. Administrative personnel authority is intended to support efficient personnel administration while preserving City Council oversight of organizational structure, staffing levels, compensation authority, labor obligations, and long-term fiscal sustainability. Appropriations Limit (Gann Limit) Policy The City shall annually calculate, adopt, and monitor its appropriations limit in accordance with Article XIIIB of the California Constitution and applicable State laws. The City shall monitor appropriations subject to limitation as part of the annual budget process to ensure ongoing compliance with State appropriations limit requirements and maintain sufficient appropriations capacity for future operational and capital needs. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Gann Appropriation Limit California voters approved Proposition 4, commonly known as the “Gann Limits” on November 6, 1979, establishing Article XIIIB of the State Constitution. This proposition mandates an appropriations (spending) limit on the amount of tax revenue that the State and most local government jurisdictions may appropriate within a fiscal year. The fundamental purpose of the Gann Limit is to keep real (inflation adjusted) per person government spending under 1978-79 levels. The State election on June 5, 1990 resulted in the passage of Proposition 111, amending Article XIIIB of the California Constitution, the governing legislation for calculating the appropriations limit. The measure requires that a complex series of calculations be performed each year to compare appropriations to the limit. Under the amended legislation, the appropriations limit may increase annually by a factor comprised of the change in population (city or county), combined with either the change in California per capita personal income or the change in the local assessment roll due to local nonresidential construction. The City used the change of City population along with the change in per capita personal income options to calculate the FY 2026 appropriation limit of $527.5 million. The City’s current FY 2026 Annual Budget includes appropriations subject to the limit of $74.2 million. This is well below the City’s appropriation limit. The City of Newark’s appropriation limit is currently over five times its annual appropriations. While Newark’s financial condition remains stable, the City continues to face increasing cost pressures associated with inflation, pension obligations, infrastructure maintenance, workforce recruitment, compensation competitiveness, cybersecurity risks, and long-term operational sustainability. The City’s budget and five-year financial forecast incorporate conservative assumptions intended to address these challenges while maintaining service levels, preserving fiscal flexibility, and supporting long-term infrastructure and organizational needs. The City will continue monitoring economic conditions, operational risks, labor market trends, infrastructure needs, and evolving service demands to maintain long-term fiscal sustainability and organizational resiliency. Inflationary Cost Pressures Inflationary pressures continue to affect both residents and municipal operations. Although inflation has moderated compared to recent post-pandemic peaks, costs for utilities, construction materials, contractual services, professional services, insurance, fleet operations, and maintenance activities continue to increase above historical averages. Energy and fuel prices remain particularly volatile due to geopolitical tensions, international conflicts, supply chain disruptions, and broader market uncertainty. These conditions continue to place upward pressure on operating and capital expenditures throughout the organization. The City’s financial forecast incorporates conservative inflation assumptions across both operational and capital expenditure categories. While most non-personnel expenditures are projected to increase approximately 3.0% annually, several expenditure categories, including utilities, insurance, public safety-related costs, and construction activities, are projected to increase at higher rates during the forecast period. Continued inflationary pressures may also affect consumer spending activity, development trends, and broader economic growth, potentially impacting economically sensitive revenues such as Sales Tax and Transient Occupancy Tax. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Priorities and Issues Infrastructure Maintenance and Capital Investment The preservation, replacement, and modernization of the City’s infrastructure continue to remain among Newark’s highest long-term priorities. Aging public infrastructure, increasing maintenance costs, deferred replacement needs, and expanding facility responsibilities continue to require significant ongoing investment. For the 2026-2028 Biennial Budget cycle, the City is transitioning from a two-year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) framework to a five-year CIP planning model to strengthen long-term infrastructure planning, project prioritization, operational coordination, grant alignment, and multi-year financial forecasting. The expanded five-year CIP framework provides a more comprehensive approach to planning and funding the City’s long-term capital and infrastructure needs while improving visibility into future project sequencing, funding strategies, operational impacts, and ongoing maintenance obligations. Major capital priorities include transportation infrastructure, pavement rehabilitation, park improvements, facility modernization, technology investments, Fire Stations 27 and 29 reconstruction, future Cultural Arts Center and community capital planning initiatives. Infrastructure maintenance and replacement activities are supported through multiple funding sources, including the General Fund Maintenance Cost Center, Equipment and Building Maintenance Internal Service Funds, capital reserves, development-related funding sources, grants, and voter-approved local revenues. The City has also completed several long-range planning initiatives, including a Facilities Master Plan, to evaluate existing assets, identify future replacement and rehabilitation needs, and support long-term capital planning efforts. These planning efforts continue to inform the City’s five-year financial forecast and future capital investment strategies. Housing affordability remains one of the most significant constraints on regional economic competitiveness. The City of Newark's Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), is a Five-Year plan that is updated on a rolling basis as part of the Biennial Budget process. Guidance on preparing the CIP comes from the City's General Plan, Specific Plans, Master Planning documents, the City's Strategic Priority Areas, direction from City Council, and community input. Capital Budgeting Process The Capital Budgeting Process (Process) establishes projects and associated budgets within the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) and utilizes a structured, transparent, and strategic approach that aligns with prudent public fiscal policies to ensure successful long-term planning, fiscal responsibility, and public accountability. The Process is interactive, dynamic, and occurs concurrently with the Biennial Budget process. The Process begins with updates and/or review of the City's Mission, Vision, Values, strategic plans, priorities and goals. This effort includes review of the City's General Plan, Specific Plans, Master Planning documents, the City's Strategic Priority Areas, direction from City Council, and community input. Potential new projects are identified with a detailed description of purpose and scope of work, rough cost estimates at time of construction, preliminary schedule, and potential funding sources. Existing CIP projects are also reviewed with estimated spending by the end of the current fiscal year ("Estimated Actuals"), updated purpose and scope of work, updated cost estimates escalated to estimated time of construction, updated schedule, and updated funding sources. Any existing CIP projects that have been completed or are nearing completion are removed from consideration. Balances, revenues, and expenditures for typical project funding as well as staffing and resources are forecasted, analyzed and reviewed within the CIP timeframe. Projects that cannot be completed within the CIP timeframe are analyzed for future funding needs beyond the CIP timeframe ("Future Budgeted"). The Process continues with the Project Ranking and Prioritization Process, whereby all projects are evaluated and scored based on established weighted criteria to determine those that may be incorporated into the Draft CIP. Projects that scored high (corresponding to a higher priority) are reviewed by the City's Executive Team. Additional evaluation considers other factors that may warrant projects to be removed from consideration. New projects may be removed or delayed from consideration if there is an upcoming study or effort that has the potential to substantially alter the project priority; if the new project is redundant or conflicts with another higher priority project; or if there isn't sufficient staffing or resources available to execute the project. The Process continues further with workshops or presentations of the draft list of projects and the Draft CIP to City Council. This provides an opportunity for City Council and the general public to review and provide feedback. The Draft CIP is also reviewed by the City's Planning Commission for conformance with the City's General Plan as required by State law. The Process is finalized with incorporation of the Final CIP into the Biennial Budget process, and formal adoption by the City Council of the Final CIP with the Biennial Budget prior to the new fiscal cycle. The adopted Biennial Budget and CIP are posted on the City's website and monitored until the Process restarts. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Capital Budgeting Process Basis for Capital Estimates Capital estimates are based on established and sound government accounting standards and practices. Estimates are based on a combination of analyzing recent and similar bid pricing, third-party expert consultant reviews, and engineering judgment. Estimates typically include contingencies consistent with the estimated amount, projected risks, and sound engineering practices. Estimates typically are escalated to represent the anticipated cost at the projected time of bidding. Capital Improvement Project Ranking and Prioritization Process Project prioritization is based on standards established by the Government Finance Officers Association. Project scores from 95 to 125 are "Critical Priority"; 70 to 94 are "High Priority"; 45-69 are "Medium Priority"; and below 45 are "Low Priority."

Section 43605 of the State of California Government Code states that a city shall not incur an indebtedness for public improvements which exceeds in the aggregate 15% of the assessed value of all real and personal property of the city. The Code section was enacted prior to the change in basing the assessed value to full market value when it was previously 25% of market value. Thus, the limit shown as 3.75% is one-fourth the limit to account for the adjustment of showing assessed valuation at full cash value. Within the meaning of this section “indebtedness” means bonded indebtedness of the city payable from the proceeds of taxes levied upon taxable property in the city. As of June 30, 2025, the City's assessed value was $15,496,518,922, therefore the debt limit for bonded indebtedness payable from tax proceeds was $145,279,865. Granted only on application of the person seeking the abatement and only by the committing governmental unit. Account: A classification of expenditure or revenue. Accounting System: The total structure of records and procedures that identify record, classify, and report information on the financial position and operations of a governmental unit or any of its funds, account groups, and organizational components. Accrual Basis Accounting: Under this accounting method, transactions are recognized when they occur, regardless of the timing of related cash receipts and disbursements. Accrued Interest: The amount of interest that has accumulated on the debt since the date of the last interest payment, and on the sale of a bond, the amount accrued up to but not including the date of delivery (settlement date). (See Interest) ACFR: Annual Comprehensive Financial Report - A detailed report of an organization's financial activities and performance over the fiscal year. Adopted Budget: The budget that is adopted by the City Council. Typically adopted by a Resolution. Adoption: Formal action by the City Council, which sets the spending limits for the fiscal year, among other items. The City’s budget is adopted by Council resolution. Amortization: The gradual repayment of an obligation over time and in accordance with a predetermined payment schedule. Appropriation: A legal authorization from the community's legislative body to expend money and incur obligations for specific public purposes. An appropriation is usually limited in amount and as to the time period within which it may be expended. Arbitrage: As applied to municipal debt, the investment of tax-exempt bonds or note proceeds in higher yielding, taxable securities. Section 103 of the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Code restricts this practice and requires (beyond certain limits) that earnings be rebated (paid) to the IRS. Assessed Valuation: A value assigned to real estate or other property by a government as the basis for levying taxes. Assets: Items owned by an organization that have economic value, such as cash, investments, property, and equipment. Audit: An examination of a community's financial systems, procedures, and data by a certified public accountant (independent auditor), and a report on the fairness of financial statements and on local compliance with statutes and regulations. The audit serves as a valuable management tool in evaluating the fiscal performance of a community. Audit Report: Prepared by an independent auditor, an audit report includes: (a) a statement of the scope of the audit; (b) explanatory comments as to application of auditing procedures; (c) findings and opinions. It is almost always accompanied by a management letter which contains supplementary comments and recommendations. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Glossary Available Funds: Balances in the various fund types that represent non-recurring revenue sources. As a matter of sound practice, they are frequently appropriated to meet unforeseen expenses, for capital expenditures or other onetime costs. Balance Sheet: A statement that discloses the assets, liabilities, reserves and equities of a fund or governmental unit at a specified date. Balanced Budget: A budget where the anticipated operating revenues and other financing resources including carryover of outstanding encumbrances from prior year are equal to or exceed operating expenditures. Betterments (Special Assessments): Whenever a specific area of a community receives benefit from a public improvement (e.g., water, sewer, sidewalk, etc.), special property taxes may be assessed to reimburse the governmental entity for all or part of the costs it incurred. Each parcel receiving benefit from the improvement is assessed for its proportionate share of the cost of such improvements. The proportionate share may be paid in full or the property owner may request that the assessors apportion the betterment over 20 years. Over the life of the betterment, one year’s apportionment along with one year’s committed interest computed from October 1 to October 1 is added to the tax bill until the betterment has been paid. Bond: A means to raise money through the issuance of debt. A bond issuer/borrower promises in writing to repay a specified sum of money, alternately referred to as face value, par value or bond principal, to the buyer of the bond on a specified future date (maturity date), together with periodic interest at a specified rate. The term of a bond is always greater than one year. (See Note) Bond and Interest Record: (Bond Register) – The permanent and complete record maintained by a treasurer for each bond issue. It shows the amount of interest and principal coming due each date and all other pertinent information concerning the bond issue. Bonds Authorized and Unissued: Balance of a bond authorization not yet sold. Upon completion or abandonment of a project, any remaining balance of authorized and unissued bonds may not be used for other purposes, but must be rescinded by the community's legislative body to be removed from community's books. Bond Issue: Generally, the sale of a certain number of bonds at one time by a governmental unit. Bond Rating (Municipal): A credit rating assigned to a municipality to help investors assess the future ability, legal obligation, and willingness of the municipality (bond issuer) to make timely debt service payments. Stated otherwise, a rating helps prospective investors determine the level of risk associated with a given fixed-income investment. Rating agencies, such as Moody's and Standard and Poors, use rating systems, which designate a letter or a combination of letters and numerals where AAA is the highest rating and C1 is a very low rating. Budget: A plan for allocating resources to support particular services, purposes and functions over a specified period of time. (See Performance Budget, Program Budget) Capital Assets: All real and tangible property used in the operation of government, which is not easily converted into cash, and has an initial useful live extending beyond a single financial reporting period. Capital assets include land and land improvements; infrastructure such as roads, bridges, water and sewer lines; easements; buildings and building improvements; vehicles, machinery and equipment. Communities typically define capital assets in terms of a minimum useful life and a minimum initial cost. Capital Budget: An appropriation or spending plan that uses borrowing or direct outlay for capital improvements. Among other information, a capital budget should identify the method of financing each recommended expenditure, i.e., tax levy or rates, and identify those items that were not recommended. (See Capital Assets) 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Glossary Cash: Currency, coin, checks, postal and express money orders and bankers’ drafts on hand or on deposit with an official or agent designated as custodian of cash and bank deposits. Cash Flow: The movement of money into or out of an organization, showing its liquidity and ability to meet financial obligations. Cash Management: The process of monitoring the ebb and flow of money in an out of municipal accounts to ensure cash availability to pay bills and to facilitate decisions on the need for short- term borrowing and investment of idle cash. Certificate of Deposit (CD): A bank deposit evidenced by a negotiable or non-negotiable instrument, which provides on its face that the amount of such deposit plus a specified interest payable to a bearer or to any specified person on a certain specified date, at the expiration of a certain specified time, or upon notice in writing. Classification of Real Property: Assessors are required to classify all real property according to use into one of four classes: residential, open space, commercial, and industrial. Having classified its real properties, local officials are permitted to determine locally, within limitations established by statute and the Commissioner of Revenue, what percentage of the tax burden is to be borne by each class of real property and by personal property owners. Collective Bargaining: The process of negotiating workers' wages, hours, benefits, working conditions, etc., between an employer and some or all of its employees, who are represented by a recognized labor union, regarding wages, hours and working conditions. Community Development Block Grant (CDBG): Federal grant funds distributed from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development that are passed through to the City. The City primarily uses these funds for housing rehabilitation, public improvements and local social programs. Compliance: Adherence to relevant laws, regulations, and internal policies governing financial reporting and operations. Consumer Price Index: The statistical measure of changes, if any, in the overall price level of consumer goods and services. The index is often called the "cost-of-living index." Cost-Benefit Analysis: A decision-making tool that allows a comparison of options based on the level of benefit derived and the cost to achieve the benefit from different alternatives. County, Federal, and State Grants: Funding or allocations by County, Federal and State agencies to support a particular program or function. Court Fines: The City’s apportionment of court fines collected and remitted by the County. Debt Burden: The amount of debt carried by an issuer usually expressed as a measure of value (i.e., debt as a percentage of assessed value, debt per capita, etc.). Sometimes debt burden refers to debt service costs as a percentage of the total annual budget. Debt Service: The repayment cost, usually stated in annual terms and based on an amortization schedule, of the principal and interest on any particular bond issue. Donations: Funds provided to the City by a private party. Encumbrance: A reservation of funds to cover obligations arising from purchase orders, contracts, or salary commitments that are chargeable to, but not yet paid from, a specific appropriation account. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Glossary Enterprise Funds: Funds used to account for operations that are financed and operated in a manner similar to a private enterprise. Examples of enterprise funds are water and sewer, which are funded directly by fee and charges to external users. Environmental Protection Fee (also known as Urban Run-Off Clean Water Fee): Charged to all parcels in the City and collected through the County tax rolls. This fee covers the City’s costs to minimize storm water runoff pollution into San Francisco Bay. This is a mandated State and Federal program. Equalized Valuations (EQVs): The determination of the full and fair cash value of all property in the community that is subject to local taxation. Equity: The residual interest in the assets of an organization after deducting liabilities, representing the owners' stake in the business. Estimated Receipts: A term that typically refers to anticipated local revenues often based on the previous year's receipts and represent funding sources necessary to support a community's annual budget. (See Local Receipts) Exemptions: A discharge, established by statute, from the obligation to pay all or a portion of a property tax. The exemption is available to particular categories of property or persons upon the timely submission and approval of an application to the assessors. Properties exempt from taxation include hospitals, schools, houses of worship, and cultural institutions. Persons who may qualify for exemptions include disabled veterans, blind individuals, surviving spouses, and seniors. Expenditure: An outlay of money made by municipalities to provide the programs and services within their approved budget. Fee: A fee is a charge, fixed by law, for the benefit of a service or to cover the cost of a regulatory program or the costs of administering a program for which the fee payer benefits. For example, professional license fees, which cover the cost of administering and regulating that category of professions are fees. Fiduciary Funds: Repository of money held by a municipality in a trustee capacity or as an agent for individuals, private organizations, other governmental units, and other funds. These include pension (and other employee benefit) trust funds, investment trust funds, private- purpose trust funds, and custodial funds. Financial Statements: Reports summarizing an organization's financial activities and position, including the balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement. Fiscal Year: The 12-month period for which an organization plans the use of its funds, typically not the same as the calendar year. Fixed Costs: Costs that are legally or contractually mandated such as retirement, FICA/Social Security, insurance, debt service costs or interest on loans. Float: The difference between the bank balance for a local government’s account and its book balance at the end of the day. The primary factor creating float is clearing time on checks and deposits. Delays in receiving deposit and withdrawal information also influence float. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Glossary Franchise Fees: A fee that is usually levied on utility companies for their use of City streets (right-of-way) or for their exclusive franchise to provide services to residents. Newark imposes a 1% tax on the gross receipts from Pacific Gas and Electric Company; a 20% tax on the gross receipts from Waste Management of Alameda County, Inc. (from both residential and nonresidential customers); a 5% tax on the gross receipts of the cable television franchise; and an annual franchise fee of approximately $6,000 on the gas pipeline that runs through Newark. Full Faith and Credit: A pledge of the general taxing powers for the payment of governmental obligations. Bonds carrying such pledges are usually referred to as general obligation or full faith and credit bonds. Fund: An accounting entity with a self-balancing set of accounts that are segregated for the purpose of carrying on identified activities or attaining certain objectives in accordance with specific regulations, restrictions, or limitations. Fund Accounting: Organizing financial records into multiple, segregated locations for money. A fund is a distinct entity within the municipal government in which financial resources and activity (assets, liabilities, fund balances, revenues, and expenditures) are accounted for independently in accordance with specific regulations, restrictions or limitations. Examples of funds include the general fund and enterprise funds. Communities whose accounting records are organized according to the Uniform Municipal Accounting System (UMAS) use multiple funds. Fund Balance: The excess of current assets over current liabilities, and represents the cumulative effect of revenues and other financing sources over expenditures and other uses. GAAP: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles - The standard framework of guidelines, rules, and procedures for financial reporting that help ensure consistency and transparency. GASB 34: A major pronouncement of the Governmental Accounting Standards Board that establishes new criteria on the form and content of governmental financial statements. GASB 34 requires a report on overall financial health, not just on individual funds. It requires more complete information on the cost of delivering value estimates on public infrastructure assets, such as bridges, road, sewers, etc. It also requires the presentation of a narrative statement the government's financial performance, trends and prospects for the future. Gasoline Tax: Gas tax revenues provided by Sections 2105, 2106, 2107, and 2107.5 of the State of California’s Streets and Highways Code. Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB): A standard-setting body, which establishes standard accounting practices for governmental units. General Fund: The fund used to account for most financial resources and activities governed by the normal appropriation process. General Obligation Bonds: Bonds issued by a municipality for purposes allowed by statute that are backed by the full faith and credit of its taxing authority. Governing Body: A board, committee, commission, or other executive or policymaking body of a municipality or school district. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Glossary Indirect Cost: Costs of a service not reflected in the operating budget of the entity providing the service. Internal Controls: Policies and procedures implemented by an organization to ensure the reliability of financial reporting and compliance with laws and regulations, aiming to prevent fraud and errors. Interest: Compensation paid or to be paid for the use of money, including amounts payable at periodic intervals or discounted at the time a loan is made. In the case of municipal bonds, interest payments accrue on a day-to-day basis, but are paid every six months. Interest Rate: The interest payable, expressed as a percentage of the principal available for use during a specified period of time. It is always expressed in annual terms. Internal Service Fund (ISF): These funds fund services provided to internal users and function on a costreimbursement basis. Internal Service Funds account for operational support activities for the purpose of recovering the cost from the user, and for the user to identify its full cost of operations. Investment Earnings: A revenue source resulting in the investment of temporary idle funds in interest-bearing accounts. Investments: Securities and real estate held for the production of income in the form of interest, dividends, rentals or lease payments. Line Item Budget: A budget that separates spending into categories, or greater detail, such as supplies, equipment, maintenance, or salaries, as opposed to a program budget. Local Aid: Revenue allocated by the state or counties to municipalities and school districts. Maturity Date: The date that the principal of a bond becomes due and payable in full. Modified Accrual Basis: Under this accounting method, revenues are recognized when they become both measurable and available to finance expenditures of the current period. Expenditures for the most part are recognized when the related fund liability is incurred except for prepayments, accumulated employee leave and long-term debt. All governmental funds and expendable trust funds are accounted for using the modified accrual basis of accounting. Municipal(s): (As used in the bond trade) "Municipal" refers to any state or subordinate governmental unit. Net Income: The difference between an organization's revenues and expenses, representing its profit or loss for a specific period. Non-Government Contribution: Reimbursement of staff costs for the administration of project consultants. 2026-2028 Biennial Budget | Newark, CA Glossary Note: A short-term loan, typically with a maturity date of a year or less. Operating Budget: A plan of proposed expenditures for personnel, supplies, and other expenses for the coming fiscal year. Performance Budget: A budget that stresses output both in terms of economy and efficiency. Principal: The face amount of a bond, exclusive of accrued interest. Secured: A property tax that is levied on real property. Real property is immobile and includes land, natural resources, and fixed improvements to the land. Unsecured: A property tax that is levied on personal property. Personal property is mobile and includes such tangible property as equipment and inventory. Proprietary Funds: Funds used to account for City activities that are similar to businesses found in the private sector. Refunding of Debt: Transaction where one bond issue is redeemed and replaced by a new bond issue under conditions generally more favorable to the issuer. Reserve Fund: An amount set aside annually within the budget of a town to provide a funding source for extraordinary or unforeseen expenditures. Revaluation: The assessors of each community are responsible for developing a reasonable and realistic program to achieve the fair cash valuation of property in accordance with constitutional and statutory requirements. Revenues: Inflows of resources or other enhancements of assets of an organization, usually from sales of goods or services. Revenue Anticipation Note (RAN): A short-term loan issued to be paid off by revenues, such as tax collections and state aid. RANs are full faith and credit obligations. Revenue Bond: A bond payable from and secured solely by specific revenues and thereby not a full faith and credit obligation. Revolving Fund: Allows a community to raise revenues from a specific service and use those revenues without appropriation to support the service. Sale of Real Estate Fund: A fund established to account for the proceeds of the sale of municipal real estate other than proceeds acquired through tax title foreclosure. Sales and Use Tax: A 10.75% sales tax is levied against the gross sales price of most tangible property sold in Newark other than property sold for resale. Senior Transportation Fee: Charged for the cost of providing transit services to seniors. The fee is subsidized by Measure B and Measure BB sales tax revenue. Stabilization Fund: A fund designed to accumulate amounts for capital and other future spending purposes, although it may be appropriated for any lawful purpose. Surplus Revenue: The amount by which cash, accounts receivable, and other assets exceed liabilities and reserves. Tax Rate: The amount of property tax stated in terms of a unit of the municipal tax base; for example, $14.80 per $1,000 of assessed valuation of taxable real and personal property. Tax Title Foreclosure: The procedure initiated by a municipality to obtain legal title to real property already in tax title and on which property taxes are overdue. Transient Occupancy Tax: A 10% tax is levied on charges for occupancy of hotel and motel rooms. Uncollected Funds: Recently deposited checks included in an account’s balance but drawn on other banks and not yet credited by the Federal Reserve Bank or local clearinghouse to the bank cashing the checks. Undesignated Fund Balance: Monies in the various government funds as of the end of the fiscal year that are neither encumbered nor reserved, and are therefore available for expenditure once certified as part of free cash. Unreserved Fund Balance (Surplus Revenue Account): The amount by which cash, accounts receivable, and other assets exceed liabilities and restricted reserves. Valuation (100 Percent): The legal requirement that a community’s assessed value on property must reflect its market, or full and fair cash value. Vehicle Code Fines: The City’s apportionment of fines and forfeitures collected by the County. These fines and forfeitures result from violations of the State Vehicle Code. Vehicle In-Lieu: Prior to the 2004 Budget Act, this revenue was backfilled from the State’s general fund.
